name: Priya Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government, and we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including what you'd keep private. What happens on a normal day in your job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead four people clearing rights for photographs and extracts at a large publishing company. We check who owns an image, what a licence permits and whether a book can use it before it goes to print. I took the manager role this summer and I'm still learning the contract exceptions; last month I approved a cover image for a second edition when its licence covered only the first. I use AI every day to find matching credit lines, but my deputy caught that mistake by reading the original licence.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is satisfying, and what is at stake at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a photographer gets paid and a book can still ship on time. I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree, and my pay is high because the rights office handles expensive releases, though I'm a beginner at leading it. My partner Karim does architectural design on contracts, so his income moves with commissions. We have a mortgage and children aged nine and twelve, but we've built about a year's expenses in savings, and there are plenty of publishers and media firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A modest tool can speed up finding credit lines, and I already use one for that. The original licence still has to be read. With our cash reserve and my high pay, the mortgage feels safe even when Karim has a quiet month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to keep opening the licence before marking an image clear. I'd tell Karim our jobs look much as they did. I would keep using the AI search to find possible matches, then check every result against the signed document.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be glad to have time to get better at this role. I made an expensive mistake on that cover, and I don't want a tool to make the same mistake faster. We have a year saved and many nearby firms, so I can own the error without fearing next month's payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd have my deputy review every second-edition licence before I sign it and add that check to the existing rights list. Through the first year of a plateau I'd keep our AI credit search as a first pass and put 300 monthly from my salary into the cash reserve when both school and mortgage bills are paid. I would not buy a new system on the promise of a few saved minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about money and slightly humbled at work. A quiet year would let me become a better manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly did your deputy spot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The image contract named one edition, but the cover spreadsheet said 'all editions'. I had looked at the spreadsheet, not the signed page. A photographer's permission is not a column someone can fill from memory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Karim's uneven work worry you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, but we budget on my salary and treat his fees as extra until they arrive. That is why the year's reserve stays in cash. I won't spend a promised commission on a school bill.

I'd tell Karim the AI search stays a **first pass**, with a person checking results.
think: I'm glad for time to fix **my own contract mistakes**.
A year's cash and **nearby firms** let me own the error without fearing next month's payment.
do: Have my deputy review **second-edition licences** before I sign them.
Keep the **existing credit search** as a first pass.
Add **300 monthly** to cash only after school and mortgage bills are paid.
feel: I feel **calm** about money and humbled by my recent error.
S0.quote: A photographer's permission is not a column someone can fill from memory.
fieldNote: The **cover licence mistake** came from trusting a spreadsheet over a signed page.
She already uses AI daily, so her credit search is **continuation**, not a new adoption.
The household budgets on **her salary** and treats Karim's fees as received, not promised.

steps.text: Have deputy review every second-edition licence before signing
Add 300 monthly to cash only after school and mortgage bills are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing permissions, checking contracts, planning releases and answering authors are exactly what the card lists. A stronger system could do the first read for four desks at once, and we might keep one person to handle disputes. Karim's drawing work could also get cheaper before any physical site visit changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our director to test the tool against licences with narrow edition limits before making staffing claims. I'd tell photographers we need a clear record of what was paid and used. I would not claim speed alone is a benefit if it creates a rights dispute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose the manager job I just got, because my deputy is better at spotting contract exceptions. I can learn a proven tool quickly, but that does not make the company need five people. Karim could lose drawing fees too, and two shrinking incomes would make our year of cash feel shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd run a paid six-week trial on old licence cases, with my deputy marking every missed edition limit. If the publisher approves, I'd keep using AI only for draft credit searches and keep staff checking signed terms before a release. I'd also ask Karim to add up fees actually paid into our account before we decide whether to cancel the summer trip; I would not spend a fee that hasn't arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about both desks at home. I can move quickly, but a clever pilot could help remove my own team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the deputy she could be kept instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell her the company may value her checks more than my new title. I can't ask her to make the trial honest and then hide the staffing risk from her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a trial failure look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it clears the second-edition cover without the photographer's permission, we stop that part. I want the error on the table, not buried in an average accuracy score. A rights dispute can cost more than a month of saved typing.

say: I'd ask for a **narrow-licence test** before any staffing claim.
I'd tell photographers they need a **paid-use record**, not just faster credit lines.
think: My **new manager post** could go even if I lead the trial.
Karim's **drawing fees** could fall too, shortening our cash runway.
do: Run a **paid six-week old-case trial** with my deputy if approved.
Keep using **AI draft credit searches** only while staff check signed terms.
Budget using only **Karim’s received fees** before deciding on the summer trip.
feel: I feel **anxious** about two incomes, despite being quick with tools.
S1.quote: A rights dispute can cost more than a month of saved typing.
fieldNote: She would tell her deputy about **possible job loss**, despite relying on her skill for the trial.
The trial tests **edition limits and permissions**, not only average speed.
She counts Karim's **confirmed fees**, rather than treating future commissions as household cash.

steps.text: Learn the new licence tool during an approved paid six-week trial
Keep using AI draft credit searches while staff check signed terms
Wait on the summer trip until Karim’s confirmed fees reach the account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could read every licence, bargain over fees and check a book faster than my office. Karim's design drawings could be done the same way, even if he still visits sites until robots around 2031. Our two main earning skills face the thinking system before any robot lifts a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell staff the date on the card and ask for written notice and paid openings. I'd tell photographers the publisher still has to prove it holds permission, even if a machine read the contract. At home I'd tell Karim we must plan for both fees and my salary to fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my rights post to go and Karim's design commissions to shrink sharply by 2028. A year of expenses in cash lets us make the mortgage while searching, but two lost incomes would drain it quickly. Nearby publishers and design firms may face the same tool, so I won't count their signs as job offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'd continue leaving Karim's unpaid commissions out of our budget and postpone the kitchen refit before paying its deposit. I'd ask our production director about a paid print-floor trial checking physical proofs and colour, with safety training and school pickup covered by Karim or another agreed adult. If approved and pickup is covered, I'd complete the trial beside a trained press worker. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my office job ends, I'd apply for a posted production vacancy only if the wage plus Karim's confirmed income covers mortgage, food and child care; otherwise I'd use the year's reserve for a wider paid search while checking any support rules before counting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the two wages. I have woken up doing the arithmetic on what a year of cash buys if both stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does print production avoid AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Its schedules, purchase orders and proof comparisons are thinking work and could change in 2028. I would need paid physical duties such as handling sheets and checking a press run, and robots arrive around 2031 in this picture. A title in the print room would not make the income safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after we put mortgage, food and childcare on one page and see what Karim has actually earned. If the trial wage fails that test, I would keep looking and use the reserve carefully. I won't let a promised design commission decide whether we buy groceries.

I'd tell photographers the publisher must prove **permission** even when AI reads licences.
think: I expect my **rights wage to end** and Karim's commissions to shrink in 2028.
A year's cash buys **time to search**, but two lost incomes would drain it.
do: Postpone the **kitchen refit** before its deposit and budget only received fees.
Complete a **paid print-floor trial** only if approved, beside a trained press worker with safety training and school pickup secured.
Apply after 2028 only for **posted physical production work** whose combined income covers bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected losses in both household incomes.
S2.quote: I won't let a promised design commission decide whether we buy groceries.
fieldNote: Her private answer expects **both earning skills** to lose value by 2028.
A print-floor move needs **physical duties** and training, childcare and adequate pay; desk tasks still face AGI.
The year's savings can bridge a search but **cannot replace two wages** indefinitely.

steps.text: Postpone the kitchen refit before paying its deposit
Complete approved paid print-floor trial beside trained press worker after safety training and pickup arrangement
Apply for posted production work only if combined confirmed income covers mortgage, food and childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let Karim and me pay down the mortgage while the rights desk still needs people. The office still faces AGI in 2031, and physical print work faces robots around 2034. I would test the floor work, but I do not want to confuse a three-year bridge with a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to ask for paid rotations that show real wages and open posts. I'd tell Karim we should keep a year's cash untouched while paying extra on the mortgage. I'd tell photographers we still owe them a verifiable licence record during any change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep my wage until 2031 and use that time to cut the mortgage balance; Karim's confirmed commissions help, but they are not guaranteed. If a print-floor role opens, I could use our cushion to accept a smaller wage for a time. Its scheduling and proof comparisons change in 2031, and the hands-on checks face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask production for two paid supervised press days each month and complete them only if the manager agrees and we cover the children's pickup. I'd send 400 extra monthly to mortgage principal while my wage covers fixed bills and our year's reserve stays intact. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd take a posted print-floor role only if its confirmed pay with Karim's covers mortgage, food and child care; if not, I'd search the other firms while drawing on savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the five-year window lets us pay down a real number. I still dislike having both pay cheques tied to thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a press day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help check colour against a signed proof and count spoiled sheets with the trained press operator. I would not touch the press controls without instruction. The physical sheets are a job; the colour comparison could be automated in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Karim's commissions fall before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 400 extra mortgage payment stops before the cash reserve gets touched. We would use my wage for food, school and the normal mortgage. I won't pay down a loan with money we haven't received.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I will be 53, our children will be nineteen and twenty-two, and we may have a much smaller mortgage. I cannot promise a paid-off house until I see the balances. My rights desk still faces AGI in 2036; press work meets robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the publisher to fund training and say exactly which jobs will remain. I'd tell friends a decade gives households with savings room to plan, but it does not give everyone the same start. I'd keep pressing for clear rights payments to photographers as the tools improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could spend several high-pay years lowering the mortgage and building a second set of practical skills. Even if I moved into print production, its paperwork faces AGI and its hands-on tasks meet robots later. With a smaller mortgage, I might choose part-time work, but only if our investments and income really cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask for a funded print safety course and a paid rotation, and if the company approves I'd finish both before considering a move. I'd keep twelve months of expenses in cash and put 500 extra toward the mortgage each month only after our fixed bills are covered by actual pay. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted production role only if its physical duties and combined confirmed wages cover our bills; otherwise I'd use the reserve for a paid search while robots remain about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the eventual change, but not trapped. Ten years lets us move the mortgage number before the job number moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our oldest would be twenty-two and the younger nineteen; I'd tell them to learn something they can show, but choose it themselves. I would not ask them to finance our mortgage. We chose that loan, not they.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest instead of paying down the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some money is already in broad funds, but I don't know which firms would win this race. I'd keep the cash year and pay down the mortgage before taking a bigger market bet. The house payment is a number I can change now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My rights checks and Karim's design drawings could both be done cheaply before either of us has another reliable income. A written notice period, a real paid opening and time to test the work would help, as would clear rules for creators whose work is used in AI systems. A year's savings gives us choices, but I don't want to mistake that for a second salary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the photographer whose image is in the book without a valid licence. The reader may never know, but that person has a bill to pay and a right to say no. A tidy credit line is not the same as permission.

headlineQuote: A tidy credit line is not the same as permission.
portrait: Priya, **43**, became a junior rights manager at a large publisher and checks image licences with four staff.
She uses **AI daily** but still misses contract exceptions; her deputy recently caught a second-edition licence error.
She and Karim have **two school-age children** and a mortgage, with a year's savings; her pay is high and his commissions vary.
Both incomes face **thinking AI early**, so she tests tools and paid options while protecting cash and creators' rights.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could sharply reduce both her rights wage and Karim's design income.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a paid opening with time to test its actual duties.
**Clear creator rights** when AI systems use photographs or other licensed work.
